hints: Look closely at the two ring diagrams and compare where the -OH, -H and -CH2OH groups point on D-glucose versus L-glucose.
Remember how an enzyme works: the substrate must fit precisely into the 3D shape of the active site to form an enzyme-substrate complex.
walkthrough:
**Compare the two shapes**

Look at D-glucose and L-glucose side by side. They have the same atoms and same ring, but the -OH and -H groups point in opposite directions. L-glucose is the mirror image shape.

Think of left and right hands, same parts but reversed.

**Recall enzyme specificity**

Enzymes are highly specific. The active site has a precise 3D shape that is complementary to only one substrate shape.

For a reaction to happen:
$$enzyme + substrate \rightarrow enzyme\text{-}substrate\ complex \rightarrow products$$

**Apply to glucose oxidase**

Glucose oxidase has an active site shaped to fit D-glucose exactly. Because L-glucose has the mirror image arrangement, its groups are in the wrong places to bond correctly.

So L-glucose does not fit into the active site, no complex forms, and no oxidation is catalysed. That is option A.

options.A: Correct. This gives the functional reason: the wrong 3D shape means L-glucose cannot fit and bind in the active site, so no enzyme-substrate complex forms.
options.B: Incorrect. Both have the same structural formula, C6H12O6. They are stereoisomers, different only in the spatial arrangement, not in the formula.
options.C: Incorrect. Being made in a laboratory does not stop an enzyme working. It is the shape that matters, not the origin.
options.D: Incorrect. This statement is true, L-glucose is the mirror image, but it only describes the molecule. It does not explain the enzyme failure like option A does.
